newsitem.title: CHINA: China says nothing new on Deng Xiaoping's health.
newsitem.headline: China says nothing new on Deng Xiaoping's health.

text.p: Chinese officials said on Tuesday nothing had changed in the health of 92-year-old Deng Xiaoping and they could not add to a similar statement issued last week.
Asked whether the health of China's paramount leader was failing, Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said: "I have nothing much to add on his health after what I said last time.
"There has been no change," Shen said.
Last week, Shen told reporters that Deng was relatively well for an old man.

Deng, whose pragmatic policies helped to transform China from a backward Stalinist state into an economic powerhouse, has not been seen in public for nearly three years. In his last appearance he looked frail and faltering.
Speculation abounds about his health, ranging from rumours he was admitted to hospital in recent days to reports he remains at home though no longer mentally alert.

The Hong Kong independent daily Ming Pao on Tuesday quoted sources from Beijing as saying Deng's son and daughters had left for a holiday on southern Hainan Island and would not have done so if their father's health had been unstable.
Deng's eldest son Deng Pufang and his daughters Deng Lin and Deng Rong had left Beijing for Hainan at the start of this month, the Ming Pao quoted its sources as saying.
It said they would return to Beijing before the Chinese Lunar New Year festival, which falls on February 7.
China Central Television's broadcasting from New Year's Day of a 12-part primetime documentary series about Deng's life had further fanned rumours about his health.
The man who launched China's economic reforms no longer holds public office but is considered highly influential.

Deng's health has long been the subject of intense speculation both in China and elsewhere because his death is expected to trigger a power struggle among those eager to succeed him as the de facto emperor of the world's most populous nation.

Deng has vowed to visit Hong Kong to witness the return of the British colony to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 but a Beijing vice-mayor believed to be close to the Deng family said recently this would be difficult.

Deng oversaw the negotiations that successfully concluded an agreement for Britain to hand back the territory it has held for 150 years. He has said repeatedly he hoped to be able to witness the historic transfer of sovereignty.

He has spent his twilight years cloistered off from the public eye, creating opportunities for power-hungry, would-be heirs fighting for his title to use his name to strengthen their hand, analysts say.
